research_concepts: minutes, initiation volume and same-position minutes as competing predictors
methodological_questions: Does the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile gain most in the absent player's primary types more often than chance and more often than simple volume heuristics?
Do most minutes, most initiations or most same-position minutes predict the largest gainer as well as or better than profile similarity?
How should 'largest gainer' be defined so that it is robust to regression to the mean, a mechanical floor and outcome-derived labels?
With 148 spells that come from only 11 cases, what is the effective sample size and power?
What baselines and placebo comparisons (non-absence games, pseudo-absences) should be used?
evidence_establishes: Nothing. The retrieval returned no records, so no historical evidence was available for this question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether this or a similar question was studied before, and with what result.
Whether the play-type derivation, the absence-spell definition or the similarity metrics have known reliability problems.
Whether any earlier approach failed, and why.
own_inferences: The 148 spells come from only 11 cases, so they are probably clustered (for example by absent player or team-season). The effective sample size is closer to 11 than to 148, and the test is underpowered for anything but a large effect.

The four predictors (closest profile, most minutes, most initiations, most same-position minutes) are likely to select the same teammate in many spells. The question is then weakly identified, and a profile-similarity effect cannot be separated from a volume effect unless the predictors disagree.

The 'largest gainer' is an argmax over noisy changes. Teammates with high baseline volume have the most room to produce a large absolute gain, so volume-based predictors may win mechanically (BASE_RATE, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, RTM_SELECTION).

Replacement players who enter the rotation, and the starter/bench structure, confound who absorbs the possessions. A teammate may gain because of lineup role changes, not because of profile similarity.
A hit rate must be compared with a chance baseline of about 1/k, where k is the number of eligible teammates in each spell. It must not be compared with 0.5 or judged on a bare count.
The question implies a single deterministic winner, so a null result is hard to interpret. The estimand should also include rank or share-of-redistribution metrics, not only top-1 matching.
uncertainties: How a 'case' differs from a 'spell' (the units give 148 spells and 11 cases), and the distribution of spells per case.
How absence spells are defined: minimum length, injury versus rest, and how partial games are handled.
How many possessions in the absent player's primary types each spell contains, and how stable those play-type labels are.
Whether the 2025-26 partial data affects any spell.
The reliability of play types derived from play-by-play (initiator and type attribution).
Which classification rules define the absent player's 'primary types' and the pre-absence profile, and whether they use only pre-absence data.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical records were returned, so the decision rests only on the task statement and my own methodological reasoning. The absence of records is not evidence that the question is new or that it was never tested.

blocking_constraints.text: The 148 spells come from only 11 cases, so the independent units are few. Only large effects over chance can be detected, and the confidence intervals will be wide.
The predictors overlap heavily, and replacement entrants and role changes drive absorption. Without spells where the predictors disagree, the profile-similarity hypothesis cannot be isolated.
Per-spell possessions in the absent player's primary types may be too few to identify a stable largest gainer.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work was retrieved, so whether the question was already answered is unknown.

risks.text: Effective n is about 11 cases, so the test is underpowered. Spells must be clustered by case, and spell-level p-values would be pseudo-replication.
The argmax of noisy per-teammate changes picks up noise. Teammates with unusually low baseline rates look like gainers through reversion.
A teammate with a baseline of zero in a type cannot lose, and high-volume players have the most absolute room to gain.
Top-minutes and top-initiation teammates are the largest gainer often by default. The hit rate needs a per-spell chance baseline of 1/k and a volume-only comparator.
Replacement players entering the rotation, other absences, opponent and schedule changes, and starter/bench structure all alter who absorbs possessions.
'Primary types' and 'largest gainer' come from the same play-type records built from play-by-play. The primary types and the similarity profile must be computed only from pre-absence games.
A profile or minutes measure that includes absence-period or later games would leak the outcome. Use only games before each spell, and freeze the 2025-26 data version.
Play-type labels are derived from play-by-play and may misattribute the initiator or type. Per-player type shares are noisy in small samples.
Four predictors, several definitions of primary type and gain metrics, and subgroups multiply the comparisons.
Play-type usage and league style change across 2022-23 to 2025-26, and within a season through trades and roster changes.
Any apparent effect needs a placebo (pseudo-absences, or a shuffled absent player) to show that it is specific to absence.

design.estimand: For each spell, the change in each eligible teammate's share of team possessions initiated in the absent player's primary types, from a pre-absence baseline to the absence period. The primary hypothesis is the within-spell probability that the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (cosine or Jensen-Shannon similarity of play-type initiation distributions) has the largest gain, compared with the 1/k chance baseline and with the most-minutes, most-initiations and same-position-minutes teammates. Secondary metrics are the rank of the predicted teammate's gain and the share of redistributed possessions absorbed.
design.unit: Absence spell, nested within case (absent player or team-season). Inference is clustered at case level.
design.sample: The 148 spells from 11 cases, 2022-23 to 2025-26, regular season and playoffs, with the data version frozen at the 2026-11-01 snapshot. Fix the spell definition, minimum games and minimum absent-player primary-type possessions before analysis. Exclude spells with multiple key absences or mid-spell trades, and report the exclusions. Define eligible teammates as those with at least a minimum number of pre-absence minutes.
design.power: With about 11 independent cases, only large effects can be detected. Before looking at outcomes, run a simulation-based power analysis using spell counts per case and the k values, and report the smallest detectable hit-rate lift over chance. If power for a pre-specified lift is below 0.8, label the result exploratory and report effect sizes and intervals, not a verdict.
design.controls: Compute the primary types and the similarity profile only from games before the spell, with a minimum possession count and shrinkage of noisy shares toward the team mean. Use a baseline window of equal length or a fixed number of games before the absence. Adjust for the replacement entrant's role, baseline volume and starter status, and for opponent strength. Include a volume-only model and test whether profile similarity adds predictive value in spells where the predictors disagree. Use a per-spell permutation baseline that respects k.
design.falsification: Placebo spells: pseudo-absences in games where the player is present, with a random matched player treated as absent, or the absent player's identity shuffled within team-season. Profile similarity should show no advantage there. Also run a negative-control play type that the absent player did not initiate. The hypothesis is refuted if the closest-profile hit rate is not above chance, or is not above the volume-only comparators, in spells where the predictors disagree.
design.multiplicity: One primary test (closest profile versus 1/k at case-clustered level). The three volume predictors and secondary metrics are confirmatory comparisons with Holm correction. Any alternative definitions are labelled exploratory and reported in full.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the case-clustered lower confidence bound on the closest-profile hit-rate lift over chance is above 0 and the profile predictor matches or beats the best volume predictor in disagreement spells, with the placebo null holding. Rejected if the upper bound is below the pre-registered minimum meaningful lift and power was adequate. Otherwise inconclusive. If the predictors agree in most spells, report the question as not separable.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files and the derived play-type graph database, 2022-23 through 2025-26 (regular season and playoffs), frozen at the 2026-11-01 snapshot. Record file hashes and the version of the play-type derivation code.

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
The retrieval came back empty, so there's no historical evidence to lean on here. I'm working out the sample: 148 absence spells spread across 11 cases, which means the effective sample for clustering is only 11, so power will be low.

I'm settling on how to judge the predictors: the hit rate against a chance baseline of 1/k, with k around 7 to 9 eligible teammates. I'm also weighing several risks, including regression to the mean, base-rate effects, confounding from lineup changes, and the fact that the sample is small and many tests are running at once.

I'm settling the analysis plan: I'll decide to proceed with some changes, and I've put rough probabilities on the outcomes, with "supported" and "uncertain" the most likely and "rejected" the least. The data is frozen as of November 1, 2026, with the 2025-26 season complete, so I'll write the design down with concrete details and keep the JSON valid.
